area: Async runtime + HTTP server stack for the webcam-handler daemon (WebSocket JSON-RPC, MJPEG-over-HTTP live preview, static web-client assets), static-asset embedding, tower middleware/graceful shutdown, and web-client technology choice (vanilla JS vs Rust-WASM frameworks)

crates.name: tokio
crates.downloads: ~860M all-time (by far the dominant Rust async runtime)
crates.maintenance: Extremely healthy: pushed to on the day of research (2026-08-07), 32.9k stars, large multi-vendor maintainer team (no bus-factor concern), LTS release policy, 444 open issues (normal for its size). MSRV 1.71, edition 2021 (freely usable from a Rust 2024 workspace — editions interop).
crates.fit: The async runtime for the daemon. Multi-threaded scheduler for concurrent WS sessions + MJPEG streams + calibration sessions; `spawn_blocking` is the right home for blocking V4L2 ioctls/DQBUF calls so device I/O never stalls the reactor; `tokio::sync::watch`/`broadcast` channels are the natural 'latest frame' fan-out primitive for MJPEG; `tokio::signal` (ctrl_c + unix SIGTERM) drives graceful shutdown. Entire axum/hyper/tower stack assumes it.
crates.native_deps: None beyond libc (pure Rust; mio uses epoll directly).
crates.caveats: Enable only needed features (rt-multi-thread, macros, sync, signal, time, net, io-util) rather than `full` to keep the daemon lean.

crates.name: axum
crates.maintenance: Maintained by the tokio-rs org (same governance as tokio/hyper/tower — strong bus factor), pushed 2026-08-07, 26.8k stars, only 75 open issues. MSRV 1.80.
crates.fit: Primary HTTP framework recommendation. (1) WebSocket: built-in via the `ws` feature — `WebSocketUpgrade` extractor + `on_upgrade`, tungstenite-based, `WebSocket` implements Stream+Sink and splits for concurrent read/write; ideal for the JSON-RPC endpoint. (2) MJPEG multipart/x-mixed-replace: a plain handler returning a Response with `Content-Type: multipart/x-mixed-replace; boundary=frame` and `axum::body::Body::from_stream(stream_of_Bytes)`; because hyper polls the body only as the client socket drains, per-connection backpressure is inherent — combine with a `tokio::sync::watch` latest-frame channel so slow clients drop frames instead of buffering (this is the standard, well-trodden pattern; scottlamb/multipart-stream-rs documents the wire format used by IP cameras). (3) Static assets: tower-http ServeDir for disk or a ~20-line rust-embed handler for embedded. (4) Graceful shutdown: `axum::serve(listener, app).with_graceful_shutdown(signal_future)` stops accepting and waits for in-flight connections. Handlers are plain async fns sharing `State<Arc<AppState>>` — trivially wraps the core library's camera manager.
crates.caveats: Still 0.x — 0.7→0.8 had breaking router/extractor changes; pin the minor version. `with_graceful_shutdown` waits for in-flight connections, and an infinite MJPEG/WS stream never finishes — you must additionally cancel long-lived stream tasks (CancellationToken selected inside the frame loop) and/or wrap shutdown in a `tokio::time::timeout`, or the daemon will hang on exit while a browser tab is open. WebSockets/multipart/compression are separate features/crates by design (assembly-required philosophy).

crates.name: tower
crates.fit: The `Service`/`Layer` middleware abstraction axum is built on. We mostly consume it transitively; directly useful utilities: `timeout`, `limit` (concurrency caps on capture-triggering endpoints), `ServiceBuilder` for composing layers once for the whole router.
crates.caveats: None material. Use the `util` + `timeout` features only.

crates.name: tower-http
crates.fit: Batteries for axum: `CorsLayer` (needed if the web client is ever served from a dev server on another port; for same-origin serving it can be permissive-localhost-only), `ServeDir`/`ServeFile` with correct ETag/Range/mime handling for disk-based assets during development, `TraceLayer` for request logging, `CompressionLayer` (do NOT apply to the MJPEG route), `SetResponseHeaderLayer` for cache-control on embedded assets.
crates.caveats: ServeDir serves from disk, not from embedded data — for single-binary deployment pair with rust-embed instead; keep ServeDir as the dev-mode path.

crates.name: tokio-tungstenite
crates.maintenance: Active (release + push July 2026), 2.5k stars, 17 open issues. MSRV 1.85.
crates.fit: WebSocket CLIENT for the daemon's CLI client crate (connect_async to the daemon's JSON-RPC endpoint). The server side does not need it directly — axum's `ws` feature wraps tungstenite itself. Using tungstenite on both ends keeps one WS implementation in the tree.
crates.native_deps: None (no TLS needed for localhost; avoid native-tls features).
crates.caveats: Version must be compatible with the tungstenite version axum's `ws` feature uses to deduplicate the dependency; check `cargo tree` when pinning.

crates.name: tokio-util
crates.downloads: part of tokio-rs; hundreds of millions
crates.fit: `CancellationToken` + `TaskTracker` are the recommended graceful-shutdown pattern: clone a token into every MJPEG frame loop, WS session, and calibration task; on SIGINT/SIGTERM cancel the token, `tracker.close(); tracker.wait()` with a timeout, then let axum's `with_graceful_shutdown` resolve. Solves the 'infinite stream never ends' problem cleanly.

crates.name: hyper
crates.maintenance: Extremely healthy; seanmonstar + large contributor base.
crates.fit: Transitive foundation of axum (and warp). Not used directly, but its poll-driven Body model is what gives every streaming response real backpressure. Listed so the design doc records the full HTTP stack: tokio -> hyper 1.x -> tower -> axum.

crates.name: rust-embed
crates.maintenance: Actively released (July 2026) but a governance yellow flag: single maintainer (pyrossh) who moved the repository off GitHub to a personal self-hosted forge (verified reachable, HTTP 200). MSRV 1.80.
crates.fit: Primary pick for embedding the web client into the daemon binary. Derive macro embeds a folder tree; killer feature for us: in debug builds it reads files from disk at runtime (instant edit-refresh web dev loop) and only embeds in release builds — include_dir has no equivalent. Optional built-in compression and mime-guess metadata. Serving through axum is a ~20-line handler (match path against `Asset::get`, set mime + long cache headers); the small `axum-embed` adapter crate exists but is trivial to inline instead.
crates.caveats: The repo move + solo maintainer means audit updates when bumping; mitigations: the API surface is tiny, the crate is build-time only (no runtime attack surface beyond file contents), and include_dir is a drop-in-ish fallback. License verified MIT on crates.io.

crates.name: include_dir
crates.maintenance: Dormant-but-stable: last release June 2024, last push July 2024, 395 stars, 37 open issues. Small, essentially feature-complete (`include_dir!` is a recursive `include_bytes!`). MSRV 1.64.
crates.fit: Fallback embedding choice. Simpler and zero-magic; fine if rust-embed's governance becomes unacceptable. You lose the debug-mode disk fallback and must write your own mime-type + caching headers (use `mime_guess`, MIT).
crates.caveats: No dev-mode hot serving; embeds in debug builds too (slower incremental builds when assets change).

crates.name: actix-web
crates.fit: Evaluated as the main axum alternative. Fully capable for our needs: `actix-ws` for WebSockets, `HttpResponse::streaming` for MJPEG, `actix-files`/`actix-web-static-files` for assets, best-in-class raw throughput (~10-15% over axum in benchmarks — irrelevant for a localhost camera daemon). NOT chosen: it layers its own runtime model (actix-rt: single-threaded worker runtimes, `!Send` handlers, `spawn_local`) on top of tokio, which makes sharing one multi-threaded camera/state core with non-HTTP daemon tasks awkward; its middleware ecosystem is separate from tower, so we'd forgo tower-http; heavier dependency tree.
crates.native_deps: None (pure Rust unless openssl features enabled).
crates.caveats: Ecosystem split with the tokio/tower stack is the disqualifier, not quality.

crates.name: warp
crates.maintenance: Alive but slow: ~1-2 releases/year (0.4.1/0.4.2 Aug 2025, 0.4.3 May 2026), 10.4k stars, 232 open issues, effectively one core maintainer (seanmonstar, whose attention is primarily hyper/reqwest).
crates.fit: Has everything we need technically (built-in websockets, `reply::stream()` added in 0.4.3, tower compatibility via wrappers). NOT chosen: the filter-combinator API produces notoriously opaque compile errors and awkward state-sharing; community momentum and third-party examples have consolidated on axum, which covers the same hyper/tokio foundation with better docs and team backing.

crates.name: poem
crates.maintenance: Repo active (pushed 2026-08-03) but last crates.io release >12 months old; 4.4k stars, 191 open issues; bus factor ~1 (sunli829). MSRV 1.85, already Rust 2024 edition.
crates.fit: Pleasant batteries-included design: built-in WebSocket, SSE, static files AND first-party rust-embed integration (`EmbeddedFilesEndpoint`) — on paper the best feature match. NOT chosen: an order of magnitude fewer users than axum, essentially one maintainer, smaller middleware/examples ecosystem, and a slowing release cadence; for a project others will maintain from a design doc, axum's ubiquity wins.
crates.caveats: Reasonable fallback if axum is rejected for taste reasons.

crates.name: axum-server
crates.fit: Only needed if the daemon ever wants TLS (rustls) or hot cert reload. For a localhost daemon, plain `axum::serve` over a TcpListener (or a Unix socket) suffices — listed as optional future add-on only.

crates.name: leptos
crates.maintenance: Very active (pushed 2026-08-07), 21.2k stars, 127 open issues, healthy contributor base. MSRV 1.88, edition 2024.
crates.fit: Best-in-class Rust-WASM option if the team insists on Rust end-to-end: fine-grained reactivity, client-side-rendering-only mode (no SSR server integration needed — the daemon just serves the wasm bundle), builds with trunk (0.21.14 stable, MIT/Apache-2.0) + wasm-bindgen (0.2.126, MIT OR Apache-2.0). All licenses permissive. NOT the primary recommendation for this project — see recommendation field: a modest control panel does not repay the trunk/wasm toolchain, several-hundred-KB payloads, and 0.x API churn (0.7->0.8->0.9 each broke signal APIs).
crates.native_deps: Build-time: wasm32-unknown-unknown target + trunk + wasm-bindgen-cli (external build tools, no linked native libs).
crates.caveats: If chosen, pin trunk and wasm-bindgen versions in CI; MJPEG preview would still be a plain tag either way.

rejected.name: async-std
rejected.reason: Officially discontinued March 2025 (RUSTSEC-2025-0052); maintainers recommend smol or tokio. License was fine (MIT OR Apache-2.0) but the project is dead. Hard reject.

rejected.name: smol
rejected.reason: Good crate, permissive (MIT OR Apache-2.0), but last release Sept 2024 and the entire server stack we want (axum/hyper services, tower, tokio-tungstenite, tower-http) is tokio-first; choosing smol buys nothing and costs ecosystem compatibility. Reject on fit.

rejected.name: actix-web
rejected.reason: Not chosen (fully evaluated above): its actix-rt runtime layer (single-threaded workers, !Send handlers) and non-tower middleware ecosystem complicate sharing one multi-threaded camera core across HTTP and non-HTTP daemon tasks; raw-throughput edge is irrelevant for a localhost daemon. License fine.

rejected.name: warp
rejected.reason: Not chosen (evaluated above): filter-combinator API with poor compile errors, ~1 maintainer, 1-2 releases/year, community consolidated on axum over the identical tokio/hyper foundation. License fine.

rejected.name: poem
rejected.reason: Not chosen (evaluated above): best on-paper feature fit (built-in WS/SSE/rust-embed endpoints) but ~1 maintainer, 5.4M downloads vs axum's 416M, last release >1 year old. Named fallback, not primary. License fine.

rejected.name: rouille
rejected.reason: Sync thread-per-request framework; last release April 2023, author (tomaka) inactive on it; websocket support exists but is rudimentary; no async backpressure story for many concurrent MJPEG viewers. Abandonment + fit reject. License fine (MIT/Apache-2.0).

rejected.name: tiny_http
rejected.reason: The 'minimal-dependency' option evaluated: sync, last release Oct 2022, last push Aug 2024, no WebSocket support (would need hand-rolled upgrade + a separate WS crate), thread-per-connection streaming only. Our daemon's WS JSON-RPC requirement alone disqualifies it. License fine.

rejected.name: static-files
rejected.reason: Permissively licensed (Unlicense OR MIT) and alive (0.3.1, Aug 2025) but it is a build.rs companion designed around actix-web-static-files, with only ~1.25M downloads; pointless outside the actix ecosystem we are not using. Poor fit.

rejected.name: multipart-stream
rejected.reason: Scott Lamb's multipart/x-mixed-replace (de)serializer — correct domain fit and permissive (MIT/Apache-2.0), but frozen at 0.1.2 since May 2021 with 13k downloads. The MJPEG framing is ~30 lines of code; write it in-house using this crate/RFC as the reference rather than depending on an unmaintained crate.

rejected.name: yew
rejected.reason: WASM framework, MIT OR Apache-2.0, still releasing (0.23.0, Mar 2026) but VDOM architecture and community momentum have been eclipsed by leptos/dioxus; if we went WASM at all, leptos is the stronger pick. Also rejected for the same build-complexity reasons as all WASM options.

rejected.name: dioxus
rejected.reason: Very active (38.5k stars, 0.7.10 July 2026, MIT OR Apache-2.0) but oriented toward its own `dx` CLI/tooling universe and cross-platform rendering — heavier conceptual footprint than the project needs; rejected with the general anti-WASM-for-this-UI rationale. Would be reconsidered only if a desktop app were ever wanted.

rejected.name: sycamore
rejected.reason: MIT, technically sound fine-grained-reactivity WASM framework, but small community (3.3k stars, ~300k downloads, last release Sept 2025) — bus-factor risk for a UI we want others to maintain. Reject.

rejected.name: rocket
rejected.reason: Not in the evaluation shortlist and not competitive here: release cadence historically slow and websocket/streaming story weaker than axum's; noted only for completeness since design-doc readers may ask.

recommendation: RUNTIME: tokio 1.x (MIT) — no viable competitor: async-std is officially discontinued (RUSTSEC-2025-0052), smol has no server-stack ecosystem. Use spawn_blocking for V4L2 ioctls, tokio::sync::watch for latest-frame fan-out, tokio::signal for SIGINT/SIGTERM. HTTP FRAMEWORK: axum 0.8 (MIT) as primary — same tokio-rs governance as the runtime, built-in `ws` WebSocket for JSON-RPC, MJPEG via a handler returning `Body::from_stream` with `Content-Type: multipart/x-mixed-replace; boundary=frame` (hyper's poll-driven bodies give inherent per-connection backpressure; pair with a watch channel so slow clients skip frames), tower + tower-http 0.7 for CORS/tracing/static-dev-serving, graceful shutdown via `axum::serve(...).with_graceful_shutdown(...)` PLUS tokio-util CancellationToken/TaskTracker to terminate infinite streams (without this the server waits forever on open MJPEG/WS connections — bake this into the design doc). Fallback framework: poem 3.x (best feature fit, weaker community) — actix-web only if someone mandates it, accepting the tower-ecosystem split. CLI client WS: tokio-tungstenite 0.30 (MIT). STATIC EMBEDDING: rust-embed 8.x (MIT) primary — its debug-builds-read-from-disk mode gives a real web dev loop and release builds are single-binary; serve via a small hand-written axum handler (skip the axum-embed micro-crate). Fallback: include_dir 0.7 (MIT, dormant-but-stable) + mime_guess. Reject static-files (actix-oriented). WEB CLIENT: plain HTML + CSS + vanilla ES-module JavaScript, no framework and no build step — the three UI jobs are trivially covered by platform APIs: MJPEG preview is literally ``, JSON-RPC is a native `WebSocket` + `JSON.stringify` with a ~50-line id-correlation helper, and controls are ``/`
risks: 1) Shutdown hang: axum's with_graceful_shutdown waits for in-flight connections, and MJPEG/WS connections are infinite — the design MUST cancel stream loops via CancellationToken and bound shutdown with a timeout, or Ctrl-C hangs while a browser tab is open. 2) Slow-consumer latency: per-connection backpressure means a slow browser would watch increasingly stale frames if the producer queues; the frame source must be a latest-value watch/broadcast channel that drops frames, and the capture task must never block on HTTP consumers. 3) rust-embed governance: solo maintainer who moved the repo off GitHub to a self-hosted forge (pyrossh.dev — verified live); license remains MIT and releases are current (8.12.0, July 2026), but pin versions, review diffs on bump, and keep include_dir as the named fallback. 4) axum is still 0.x: 0.7->0.8 broke routing syntax; pin minor version and expect a mechanical migration roughly yearly. 5) Version alignment: axum's `ws` feature embeds a specific tungstenite version — keep tokio-tungstenite (CLI client) on the matching version or two copies compile in. 6) tower-http CompressionLayer must exclude the MJPEG route (compressing multipart/x-mixed-replace breaks progressive rendering and adds latency). 7) MJPEG framing is hand-written (the only maintained option); it is ~30 lines but needs a test against real browsers (Chrome/Firefox both render multipart/x-mixed-replace in ; Safari support has historically been flaky — flag Safari as a compatibility caveat, with a JPEG-poll or WS-binary-frame fallback as the documented escape hatch). 8) No native/system library dependencies exist anywhere in the recommended stack (all pure Rust, no TLS needed for localhost), so the hard license constraint is satisfied end-to-end: every recommended crate is MIT, MIT OR Apache-2.0, or (static-files, rejected anyway) Unlicense OR MIT; all verified on crates.io on 2026-08-07, with htmx additionally verified 0BSD against its repository LICENSE. MSRV ceiling of the recommended set is 1.88 (none conflict with a Rust 2024 workspace, which already requires 1.85+; edition mixing is a non-issue in Cargo).
